Feebleminded
fē´bl-mīnd-ěd
adj. (fainthearted; small-souled under pressure — not defective in intellect)
From feeble + minded. Paul's Greek is oligopsuchos, small-souled — the discouraged and fainthearted. The English word has since narrowed to mean intellectual disability, which the Greek does not mean at all.

Biblical Definition

Paul gives a congregation four different duties toward four different kinds of member, and the differences matter: “Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). The unruly get a warning; the fainthearted get comfort; the weak get a prop under them; and everyone gets patience. Treating the fainthearted man as though he were unruly — scolding a discouraged soul — is a failure of pastoral care, and so is comforting a man who needs to be warned. Paul repeats the burden on those who can bear it: “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Romans 15:1). The pattern is Christ's own, prophesied by Isaiah: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth” (Isaiah 42:3), and Matthew records the fulfilment in the middle of a Sabbath controversy: “A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory” (Matthew 12:20). A reed already bruised and a wick already smoking are the two things easiest to finish off, and He does not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines feeble-minded as weak in mind; wanting firmness or constancy; irresolute — the older sense of faintheartedness rather than intellectual defect.

expand to see more

FEEBLE-MINDED, a. Weak in mind; wanting firmness or constancy; irresolute.

FEEBLE, a. [Fr. faible.] Weak; destitute of much physical strength; wanting force or vigor.

FAINT-HEARTED, a. Cowardly; timorous; dejected; easily depressed, or yielding to fear.

COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen the mind under affliction; to console; to give new vigor to the spirits.

SUPPORT, v.t. [L. supporto.] To bear; to sustain; to uphold; to keep from falling.

Key Scripture

1 Thessalonians 5:14 — "Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men."

Romans 15:1 — "We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves."

Isaiah 42:3 — "A bruised reed shall he not break, and the smoking flax shall he not quench: he shall bring forth judgment unto truth."

Matthew 12:20 — "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory."

Modern Corruption

An English word that has shifted since 1611 makes a tender apostolic command sound like a slur, and the distinct pastoral duty it names is lost.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The problem is a genuine shift in English. Feebleminded now means intellectually disabled, and a modern reader hears Paul categorizing people cruelly. His oligopsuchos means small-souled — the discouraged, the fainthearted, the believer whose courage has run out. The principle to recover is that 1 Thessalonians 5:14 names four distinct pastoral duties, and the value of the verse lies entirely in not confusing them.

The practical failure is common and costly. A congregation with one register — all exhortation, or all comfort — will damage half its members. The unruly man treated tenderly is confirmed in his disorder; the fainthearted man warned is crushed by the very people who should have strengthened him. Isaiah 42:3 is the standard, and it is set in a prophecy about a King bringing forth judgment: He is not indulgent, and He does not break what is already bent. A church that can only rebuke has not learned the first thing about the Servant it preaches.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek oligopsuchos (G3642), small-souled, fainthearted; paramutheomai (G3888), to comfort, encourage; antechomai (G472), to hold firmly to, support; ataktos (G813), disorderly.

expand to see more

Greek oligopsuchos (G3642) — small of soul, fainthearted; only 1 Thessalonians 5:14.

Greek ataktos (G813) — out of rank, unruly; the ones to be warned, not comforted.

Greek paramutheomai (G3888) — to speak near, encourage; the duty owed the fainthearted.

Greek antechomai (G472) — to cling to, hold up; the prop under the weak.

Hebrew qaneh ratsuts (H7070 + H7533) — a bruised reed; Isaiah 42:3.

Usage

"“Warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded” — and never the reverse."

"“Bear the infirmities of the weak” — the burden falls on the strong."

"“A bruised reed shall he not break” — the standard, and He is the King."
